49847: The kingdom has come in Jesus, so his people now live by its ethic. Past judgements were real acts of God’s justice; final judgement remains, and belongs to God, which frees believers to love enemies (Rom 12:19-21).
49850: Rabbis also read “eye for an eye” as monetary compensation, not literal maiming. Jesus’ teaching stands within Jewish debates about mercy, while making a strong call to non-retaliation.
49852: Phrase used widely in his preaching; also the title of his book *Jesus Christ Is Perfect Theology* (2016)
49853: If a reading of Scripture gives you a Father who is unlike the Son, your reading is incorrect. Scripture bears witness to the Word; it is not the Word himself (John 5:39–40). Jesus is the measure that measures all.
49854: Now reverse all three: in Jesus, the human is fully known, the Father is fully known, and creation’s future is fully known. God is not hiding behind mystery. He is unveiling in the Son.
49855: Jesus is perfect theology (cruciform Jesus lens)
49856: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Eric Seibert (in a stronger form), Tommy Miller, Bill Johnson (the phrase)
49857: Jesus, and above all the cross, is the full and final revelation of God. Any portrait of God, including in Scripture, must be measured by him. Old Testament portraits that do not look like Jesus are read as God accommodating himself to his people’s partial perceptions.
49858: Builds directly on John 1:18, John 14:9, Heb 1:3 and Col 2:9; offers a coherent way to read violent texts; gives believers confidence that God is good; echoes church fathers such as Origen and Gregory of Nyssa who read some texts spiritually because they seemed unworthy of God.
49859: Risk of Marcionism; Jesus himself affirmed the Old Testament and spoke of judgement; the New Testament has its own judgement texts; the criterion of “Christlikeness” may be shaped by the reader’s values.
49861: Graeme Goldsworthy, Edmund Clowney, Christopher J. H. Wright, D. A. Carson, Tim Keller
49862: Every part of Scripture points to Christ through promise, pattern and story. The Old Testament’s portrayals of God, including his judgements, are true revelation, which Christ fulfils (judgement and mercy meet at the cross).
49863: Holds the whole canon as fully true; follows Luke 24:27; keeps God’s justice and love together; strong guard against Marcionism.
49864: Jesus-lens writers say it leaves God’s character divided (Jesus loving enemies, God commanding their destruction) and can explain away the force of Jesus’ “but I say to you”.
49865: Hard texts as ancient war rhetoric
49866: Paul Copan, Matthew Flannagan, John Walton
49867: Many violent texts use the stylised, exaggerated language of ancient Near Eastern war reports, and much of the Torah improved on surrounding laws. Read in context, God is not the moral monster some suppose.
49868: Takes the ancient setting seriously; keeps the texts as true revelation while softening misreadings; based on comparative evidence.
49869: Critics on both sides say it does not remove the moral problem, only reduces it; Jesus-lens writers think it still leaves God commanding killing.
49870: Catholic and Orthodox: Christ the key, read in the church
49871: *Dei Verbum*; Origen, Augustine, Maximus the Confessor; John Behr
49872: Christ is the key that opens all Scripture, which is read in the church’s worship and in the line of the Fathers. The Old Testament contains elements that are “incomplete and temporary” yet belong to God’s pedagogy, and the spiritual sense of texts finds Christ throughout.
49873: Deep historical roots; integrates Christ-centred reading with the creeds and worship; avoids both Marcion and literalism.
49874: Protestants worry that tradition may overrule Scripture; some find allegorical readings too loose to check.
49876: The Hebrew Bible has its own integrity and was read faithfully by Jews for centuries before and after Jesus. Treating it as “partial” or “flawed perception” can echo old Christian contempt for Judaism.
49877: Calls Christians to humility and accuracy; reminds them that Jesus and the apostles were Jews reading Jewish Scripture.
49878: Christians answer that confessing Jesus as the fullest revelation is not contempt for Israel, whose Scriptures Paul calls a privilege (Rom 9:4-5).
49879: “The Word of God” always means the Bible
49880: When the Bible says “the Word of God”, it is talking about the Bible itself.
49881: In John 1 and Rev 19:13 the Word is a person, Jesus. Elsewhere “the word of God” often means God’s message preached (Acts 4:31; Acts 6:7). The Scriptures are God’s word in the sense that they bear witness to the Word and carry his message.
49882: Evangelical scholars agree that Jesus is the Word in the fullest sense, while insisting that Scripture is truly God’s word written (2 Tim 3:16; Mark 7:13), not merely a human witness.
49883: Forgetting that the Word is a person can turn Bible reading into rule-checking that never comes to Jesus for life (John 5:39-40).
49885: Anyone who reads Old Testament violence through Jesus is rejecting the Old Testament God, like Marcion.
49886: Marcion taught two different gods and cut most Scripture out of his canon. Jesus-lens writers such as Boyd and Jersak confess one God, keep the whole canon, and say the problem is in the human perception, not a different god. The charge is a real warning but not an accurate description of their view.
49887: Critics reply that, even with one God and one canon, saying some texts misrepresent God functionally does what Marcion did: it lets the reader decide which parts of Scripture really speak for God.
49888: Labels end conversations. The fair question is whether a reading keeps both one God and the authority of the whole canon.
49889: What is the difference between calling Jesus “the Word” and calling the Bible “the word of God”? Why does it matter which comes first?
49890: John says Jesus “exegeted” the Father. If you had only Jesus’ life to go on, what would you say God is like?
49891: Tommy Miller says that if a reading gives a Father unlike the Son, the reading is wrong. Where does that test help you? Where might it be hard to apply?
49892: Which objection to the Jesus lens do you find strongest: the Marcion risk, Jesus’ own high view of the Old Testament, New Testament judgement texts, or “who decides what is Christlike”? How would you answer it?
49893: How do Goldsworthy and Clowney’s Christ-centred readings differ from Boyd and Jersak’s? What does each one protect?
49894: Can you think of a time when the Bible was used in a way that was “deadly”? What would reading through Jesus have changed?
49895: Read John 1:1-18 aloud. Underline every phrase that says what the Word does, and write a one-line prayer from verse 18.
49896: Choose one hard Old Testament passage. Read it, then read a Gospel passage that shows Jesus in a similar situation. Write down what you learn from the comparison and what questions remain.
49897: With a friend who reads differently from you, take one view in the views list and try to explain it so well that its holder would say, “Yes, that is what I believe.”
